rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2-3 report the authors' own processing of 2779 DGA withdrawal-metering records, METRIC/Landsat AET rasters for 27 sites and a 98.6 km2 AOI (2019-2022), a random forest withdrawal model, and an auditing-priority raster (Figs. 6-12, Table 2).
rows.notes: The study does not test remote-sensing ET maps being used to dynamically adapt water allocation, nor any resulting resilience to seasonality or climate change. What it shows is that METRIC AET correlates moderately with reported withdrawals (R2 0.33, CCC 0.74; random forest R2 0.64), that reported withdrawals are ~20-25% of granted rights, and that AET plus distance-to-rights can prioritise auditing of unauthorised withdrawals. Linking AET to adaptive allocation is argued for in the Discussion and Conclusions, not demonstrated. This is a precondition (quantifying demand/withdrawals) for the claimed adaptive-allocation effect, so upstream.

rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2-3 report the authors' own analysis of national withdrawal-metering data, METRIC AET estimates at field and aggregated scales, and a trained random forest model (Figs. 9-11, Table 2).
rows.notes: No water conservation or water-saving outcome from remote-sensing ET maps is measured. The study only reports agreement between remote-sensing AET and metered withdrawals, field application efficiencies (median ~80%) derived from AET minus rainfall over withdrawals, and an auditing-priority map; it suggests these could target support for irrigation technologies or audit over-extraction, but no reduction in water use is demonstrated. Supports only a precondition (water accounting/auditing capability), so upstream.

notes: Full text appears complete (abstract through references). Supplementary figures S1-S7 referenced but not included; they are not needed for these ratings since neither claim's effect is tested in the study.
